summary: Jesus teaches how to win back a brother who sins, then answers Peter’s question about forgiving with a parable of a servant forgiven a debt beyond paying.
key_insight: The two debtors use almost the same words: “Have patience with me, and I will pay you all.” The servant forgiven ten thousand talents heard his own plea from a man who owed him a hundred denarii, and he did not recognize it.
story: Jesus went on teaching His disciples. “Moreover if your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother.” If he would not listen, they were to take one or two others along, so that every word would be confirmed by two or three witnesses. If he refused to hear them, they were to tell it to the church, and if he refused even the church, he was to be treated like a heathen and a tax collector.

“Assuredly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” If two of them agreed on earth about anything they asked, His Father in heaven would do it. “For where two or three are gathered together in My name, I am there in the midst of them.”

Then Peter came to Him and said, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

Then He told a story. A king decided to settle accounts with his servants, and one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. He could not pay, so his master ordered that he be sold, with his wife and children and all that he had. The servant fell down before him: “Master, have patience with me, and I will pay you all.” The master was moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the whole debt.

But that servant went out and found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii. He seized him by the throat, saying, “Pay me what you owe!” His fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, “Have patience with me, and I will pay you all.” But he would not; he had him thrown into prison until he should pay the debt.

When the other servants saw it, they were very grieved and told their master everything. The master called him in: “You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Should you not also have had compassion on your fellow servant, just as I had pity on you?” In anger the master handed him over to the torturers until he should pay all that was due.
“So My heavenly Father also will do to you,” Jesus said, “if each of you, from his heart, does not forgive his brother his trespasses.”

scene.label: Ten thousand talents
scene.text: A talent was about six thousand denarii, some twenty years’ wages for a laborer. Ten thousand was the largest number in common Greek use, and the talent the largest unit of money. Josephus says Herod Antipas drew two hundred talents a year in taxes from all of Galilee and Perea.

scene.label: A hundred denarii
scene.text: A denarius was a day’s wage (Matthew 20:2), so this was about a hundred days’ work: a real debt, but one that could be paid. The first debt was about six hundred thousand times larger.

scene.label: Sold for debt
scene.text: Selling a debtor and his family into slavery was known in the ancient world and in Israel’s own history (2 Kings 4:1). Prison for debt was common too; family and friends were expected to raise the money.

scene.label: Seven times
scene.text: Peter’s seven was generous. Some later rabbis taught that a repeated offense need be forgiven only three times. Jesus’ answer echoes Lamech’s boast of vengeance “seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4:24); whether read as seventy-seven or seventy times seven, the point is forgiveness that stops counting.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew alone records this teaching and parable, which close the fourth of his five great discourses. He sets church discipline and limitless forgiveness side by side, so that confronting a brother is never separated from a forgiving heart. The closing words, “from his heart,” echo Jesus’ teaching on forgiveness after the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12–15).

seeing.reveals: Jesus shows the King’s heart: moved with compassion, He cancels a debt that could never be paid. He also shows the King’s seriousness: a person who receives such mercy and refuses to pass it on has not understood it.
seeing.living: Every wrong done to you is a hundred denarii; what God has forgiven you is ten thousand talents. Go to the brother who sinned against you, privately and to win him back, and keep forgiving from the heart without keeping count.
seeing.ponder: Whose hundred denarii are you still holding, and have you measured them against the debt God has forgiven you?

preaching.big_idea: Those forgiven an unpayable debt must forgive from the heart, without keeping count.
preaching.watch_for: The chapter holds two things together: confronting a brother’s sin to win him back (15–20) and forgiving without limit (21–35). In context, “where two or three are gathered together” speaks first of the church acting together in such matters.
